title: (Scenario) A customer cannot access the application though credentials are correct — how do you debug end-to-end (DNS → LB/Ingress health → Service/Pod readiness → auth service → logs/traces)?
shortTitle: Debugging end-to-end when a customer cannot access the application though credentials are correct

s1_definition.profdef: End-to-end debugging of an access failure means tracing the request along the entire path it travels — DNS resolution, load balancer or ingress health, Kubernetes Service and Pod readiness, the authentication service, and finally the application logs and distributed traces — and checking each hop in order until you find the broken link. You work the layers systematically from the outside in, confirming at each boundary whether the request arrived and what response it got, so you isolate the one layer that is failing instead of guessing.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh (SAV2001) at the National Bank of India types his correct password but still cannot get in. You do not randomly poke things. You retrace his journey like a detective: did his letter even find the bank's address (DNS)? Did the front gate let him in (load balancer and ingress)? Was any teller counter actually open (Service and Pod readiness)? Did the ID-check desk verify him (auth service)? And what do the bank's CCTV logs and journey maps say (logs and traces)? You check each checkpoint in order until you find the one that is closed.
s1_definition.oneliner: Follow the request hop by hop — DNS, then load balancer and ingress, then Service and Pod readiness, then the auth service, then logs and traces — and the first hop that fails is your culprit.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** End-to-end debugging of an access failure means tracing the request along the entire path it travels — DNS resolution, load balancer or ingress health, Kubernetes Service and Pod readiness, the authentication service, and finally the application logs and distributed traces — and checking each hop in order until you find the broken link. You work the layers systematically from the outside in, confirming at each boundary whether the request arrived and what response it got, so you isolate the one layer that is failing instead of guessing.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh (SAV2001) at the National Bank of India types his correct password but still cannot get in. You do not randomly poke things. You retrace his journey like a detective: did his letter even find the bank's address (DNS)? Did the front gate let him in (load balancer and ingress)? Was any teller counter actually open (Service and Pod readiness)? Did the ID-check desk verify him (auth service)? And what do the bank's CCTV logs and journey maps say (logs and traces)? You check each checkpoint in order until you find the one that is closed.

**One line to remember:** Follow the request hop by hop — DNS, then load balancer and ingress, then Service and Pod readiness, then the auth service, then logs and traces — and the first hop that fails is your culprit.

sections.s2_technical:
Start at DNS because if the hostname does not resolve, nothing else matters. You check resolution with a lookup such as `nslookup api.nationalbank.in` or `dig api.nationalbank.in +short`, and you confirm the returned IP is the current load balancer address, not a stale record cached from an old deployment. A common failure is a DNS record pointing at a deleted load balancer, so the browser shows "correct credentials" from a cached login page but new requests go nowhere.

Next check the load balancer and ingress health. On AWS you look at the target group health in the ALB: `aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn <arn>` tells you whether targets are healthy or draining. In Kubernetes you inspect the Ingress with `kubectl describe ingress banking-ingress` and confirm the ingress controller has an address and the backend rules map the host and path to the right Service. A frequent cause is an ingress rule pointing at a Service name that was renamed, so the gate is open but it forwards to a door that no longer exists.

Then verify Service and Pod readiness. `kubectl get endpoints banking-service` shows whether the Service has any ready Pod IPs behind it; an empty endpoints list means the Service routes to nothing. `kubectl get pods -l app=banking` with `kubectl describe pod` and `kubectl logs` reveals whether Pods are CrashLoopBackOff, failing readiness probes, or OOMKilled. A Pod that is Running but not Ready (readiness probe failing) is silently removed from the Service endpoints, which perfectly matches "my password is right but the app will not load."

Next check the authentication service itself. The credentials being correct does not mean the auth service is up — it may be returning 500 because its database connection pool is exhausted, or returning 401 because a clock skew invalidated JWT signature validation, or the token-signing key was rotated and the verifying service still has the old public key. You hit the auth service's health endpoint directly and read its logs for the specific user, and you check token expiry and signature validation errors.

Finally, use logs and distributed traces to pinpoint the exact failing span. A correlation ID or trace ID attached to the request lets you follow it in Jaeger or your tracing backend across gateway, auth, and application services, and the span that errors or never starts tells you precisely where it died. Structured logs filtered by the customer's account ID, such as SAV2001, show the last successful step and the first failure. The discipline is to confirm, at each boundary, whether the request arrived and what status came back, so you convert a vague "cannot access" into a precise "readiness probe on the banking Pod is failing because the database is unreachable."
sections.s3_banking:
Rajesh (SAV2001) reports he cannot log in to the National Bank of India app even though his password is correct. We need a systematic end-to-end diagnostic that walks every hop and reports exactly which one is broken.

Problem 1 — We do not know which layer is failing. If we guess, we waste minutes while customers are locked out. This is exactly what a layered health-check pipeline solves: check each hop in a fixed order and stop at the first failure.

Problem 2 — Each layer has its own way of being healthy or unhealthy. DNS resolves or not; the load balancer has healthy targets or not; the Service has ready endpoints or not; the auth service returns a valid token or an error. We model each as a diagnostic step that returns a pass or fail with a reason.

Problem 3 — We want a single clear verdict naming the broken hop, plus the evidence, so the on-call engineer knows what to fix. Our runnable Java simulation models a `DiagnosticStep` chain (Chain of Responsibility) with concrete checks for DNS, ingress, Service readiness, and auth, and an `AccessDiagnosticEngine` that runs them in order and reports the first failing hop. Classes: `DiagnosticResult`, `DiagnosticStep`, concrete steps, `AccessDiagnosticEngine`, and an `AccessDebugDemo` main.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the diagnostic demo
java -cp target/classes com.bank.diag.AccessDebugDemo

# Real commands you would actually run during the incident
dig api.nationalbank.in +short
aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:...:targetgroup/banking/abc
kubectl get endpoints banking-service
kubectl get pods -l app=banking -o wide
kubectl describe pod banking-7d9f-xyz | sed -n '/Readiness/,/Events/p'
kubectl logs deploy/auth-service --since=10m | grep SAV2001
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a login attempt by Rajesh, account SAV2001, with correct credentials.

Step 1 — The engine starts at the DNS hop. `DnsStep` confirms `api.nationalbank.in` resolves to 10.0.5.20, which matches the expected load balancer IP, so this hop passes and we move on.

Step 2 — The engine checks the load balancer and ingress hop. `IngressStep` reports two healthy targets and a backend Service named `banking-service` that exists, so this hop passes.

Step 3 — The engine checks Service and Pod readiness. `ServiceReadinessStep` finds zero ready endpoints even though three Pods are Running — they are NotReady because their readiness probe is failing. This hop FAILS. The engine logs the root cause and stops immediately, because checking the auth service would be pointless when no Pod is receiving traffic.

Step 4 — The engine never reaches the auth hop. It returns a verdict naming `Service/PodReadiness` as the broken hop, with the evidence that readiness probes are failing, which points the on-call engineer at the Pod's dependency (the database) as the real fix.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 02:05:11 [INFO   ] Starting end-to-end access diagnosis for SAV2001
2026-10-30 02:05:11 [INFO   ]   [OK]   DNS: resolves to 10.0.5.20
2026-10-30 02:05:11 [INFO   ]   [OK]   LoadBalancer/Ingress: 2 healthy targets, backend=banking-service
2026-10-30 02:05:11 [SEVERE ]   [FAIL] Service/PodReadiness: Service has 0 ready endpoints; 3 pods in phase Running (NotReady) (readiness probe failing)
2026-10-30 02:05:11 [SEVERE ] ROOT CAUSE at hop 'Service/PodReadiness'. Fix this before checking later hops.
2026-10-30 02:05:11 [INFO   ] VERDICT: broken hop = Service/PodReadiness | healthy=false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Rajesh (SAV2001) logs in with CORRECT password
    │
    ▼
  [Hop 1] DNS  api.nationalbank.in → 10.0.5.20 (matches LB)
    │
    ▼
  [Hop 2] LoadBalancer/Ingress  2 healthy targets, backend=banking-service
    │
    ▼
  [Hop 3] Service/Pod Readiness
    │  kubectl get endpoints banking-service → 0 ready
    │  3 pods Running but NotReady (readiness probe failing: DB unreachable)
    │ FAIL — STOP HERE
    ▼
  [Hop 4] AuthService  ── never reached ──
    │
    ▼
  VERDICT: broken hop = Service/PodReadiness
  Fix: restore DB connectivity so readiness probe passes → endpoints repopulate
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When a customer reports they cannot access the application even though their credentials are correct, I debug end-to-end by following the request along its entire path and checking each hop in a fixed order, because the correct password tells me the problem is almost certainly in the infrastructure rather than the user. I start at DNS and confirm the hostname resolves to the current load balancer address and not a stale record, because a wrong or cached DNS entry sends every request into a void. Then I check the load balancer and ingress — on AWS I look at the ALB target group health, and in Kubernetes I describe the ingress to confirm it has an address and routes the host and path to the right Service.

Next I verify Service and Pod readiness, which is where these issues most often hide. I run a check on the Service endpoints, and if the endpoints list is empty the Service is routing to nothing even though Pods may show as Running, because a failing readiness probe silently removes a Pod from the Service. That single fact — Running but NotReady — perfectly explains a login page that loads from cache while every real request fails. Only after that do I check the authentication service itself, because correct credentials do not mean the auth service is healthy; it might be returning 500 because its database pool is exhausted, or rejecting valid tokens because a signing key was rotated and the verifier still holds the old public key.

Finally I use structured logs filtered by the customer's account ID and distributed traces keyed on a correlation ID to pinpoint the exact failing span across gateway, auth, and application. In my project at the National Bank of India, when Rajesh with account SAV2001 could not log in, this exact method took me from a vague complaint to a precise root cause in minutes: DNS and ingress were healthy, but the banking Service had zero ready endpoints because the Pods' readiness probes were failing against an unreachable database. The principle I always state is to confirm at every boundary whether the request arrived and what status came back, work from the outside in, and stop at the first hop that fails — that is the broken link, and fixing it restores service without touching the healthy layers.
